issues.explanation: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events are not well linked to the stated trauma of witnessing childhood domestic violence, especially when the other trigger items center on male presence and shouting. This trigger is not impossible, but in this profile it stands out as insufficiently connected to the rest of the formulation.

Listening for signs that someone is entering the home suggests a burglary/home-intrusion threat theme, which is weakly connected to the selected trauma-specific cues and memory/appraisal content centered on domestic violence. It pulls the threat profile toward external break-in danger rather than reenacted interpersonal violence.

Noticing weapons or dangerous objects in any environment implies a generalized weapon-attack threat theme, but the trauma type and the rest of the items do not support a weapon-focused formulation. This makes the threat node less coherent with the memory and appraisal content.

'I have failed in my most important role in life' is a broad role-failure appraisal that is not clearly anchored to the selected trauma memories or other appraisals. The other negative appraisals emphasize weakness and disconnection; this item introduces a different theme without enough support elsewhere in the profile.

Drug use is not well supported by the rest of the five-component profile. The strongest formulation link is Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies, and the other strategies clearly fit trigger-driven internal threat management, whereas drug use introduces a more severe coping pattern without corresponding support from the other selected items.

vignette: Miguel, a 64-year-old jeweler of Mexican descent, sits at the edge of his workshop, hands steady over a tiny loupe, yet his eyes flick from polished gold to the faint scar on his forearm that still reminds him of a night long ago. He had watched his mother cry as her husband's fists struck the kitchen table, the echoing shouts ricocheting through the cramped apartment. The memory is not a single, fluid story but a series of vivid, snapshot images that flash when the sound of a raised voice or the sight of a man's silhouette passes by. He has carried that fragment of terror for decades, and it has shaped how he now reacts to ordinary sounds, to other men, and to any hint of confrontation. When a neighbor's voice rises in the hallway, Miguel's mind jumps immediately to that old kitchen scene. The shouting acts as a trigger that pulls him into a defensive loop: he avoids any moment that might feel like a pause, such as leaning back in his chair to relax after a finished piece, because that stillness feels like a vulnerability. The trigger also sharpens his vigilance, prompting him to scan his surroundings for weapons-knives tucked behind display cases, screwdrivers that might be used as daggers. Simultaneously, the sudden noise triggers his sense that he has failed in his most important role; a jeweler whose work requires precision and calm, yet he feels as though his craft is compromised by his own terror. Miguel's constant monitoring of his thoughts has become a strategy to prevent the feeling that he is "going crazy." He checks his mind for any sign that he is slipping, and when he hears a shout, he instinctively thinks, "I must be watching, I must be prepared." This thought-monitoring is a maladaptive strategy that both pulls him deeper into the memory-he relives the kitchen scene each time he checks-and reinforces his belief that he is weak and has failed. By trying hard not to dwell on the violence, he actually suppresses the memory's surface, but the suppression itself fuels the vividness of the remaining images and the guilt that gnaws whenever he recalls the night. The act of trying to keep the trauma at bay paradoxically keeps the traumatic memory alive in his mind, and each attempt to suppress it reinforces the feeling that he cannot trust himself. His awareness that danger could be concealed in any ordinary object-whether a butter knife in a drawer or a small screwdriver on a workbench-keeps his senses constantly heightened. The inability to trust safety is so pervasive that even when a coworker says, "Everything's fine here," Miguel refuses to believe it. Watching others closely for any sign of harm becomes an automatic response; he scans a colleague's face for subtle tension, and any sudden change sends a ripple of anxiety through his body. This hypervigilance strengthens his negative appraisal of himself as weak, and the belief that he is unable to protect himself or others at work only deepens his fear of confrontation. Miguel's sense of loss is more than the absence of a partner; he feels he has lost the community that once supported him. He once shared his craft with other jewelers in a local guild, but after the divorce, the meetings became a reminder of the life he feels he has failed. The loneliness compounds his self-belief that he is inadequate, and the lack of communal support feeds into his perception that he is isolated and alone in his struggle. Each time he recalls the violent night, he feels guilt, as though he could have prevented it, and that guilt further erodes his confidence in his role as a craftsman and a man. The web of reactions is tight. Triggers-shouting, being around men, conflict-push Miguel toward avoidance of relaxation, heightened threat perception, and negative beliefs. Those same beliefs then heighten threat perception and reinforce the triggers he has learned to fear. The memory, vivid and snapshot-like, feeds both the avoidance and the threat; it keeps him locked in a cycle of thought monitoring and suppression that only serves to keep the traumatic images fresh and his sense of failure ever-present. Watching others, the constant threat of a hidden weapon, and the inability to trust safety become the scaffolding upon which his self-critical narrative stands. Now, years later, Miguel is in a small, cramped apartment with a worn bench and a few prized gemstones. He finds himself unable to sit on the bench for more than a few seconds; the simple act of resting feels dangerous. The same day he receives a notification from a former guild member that a meeting is resuming, his heart races; the thought that he might be unable to attend, that he might again feel lost, overwhelms him. It is this mounting fear of being judged, of confronting men, and of re-experiencing the violence in even the quiet moments of his shop that has finally pushed him to seek help. He hopes that, through therapy, he can break the loop that has made his daily craft feel like a battlefield, and he fears that if he does not, the memory of that old kitchen, the guilt he carries, and the sense that he is a failed man will continue to erode the only steady place he has ever known.
